[33.2] Now, I shall further explain the cultivation of the mandala of speech:
one should first cultivate the outer [mandala] in the center of the primary mandala.
The eastern lotus is eight-spoked and red in color;
likewise, from the transformation of Vajrasattva, there is the visualization of Vāgvajra.
Four-faced and twelve-armed, standing in the *ālīḍha* posture,
he embraces Padmaḍākinī, [experiencing] the sublime bliss of great passion.
Padmaghaṇṭā embraces Maheśvara, who wears a severed head;
she has produced the skin of Maheśvara and spreads it out with both hands.
The remainder [should be understood] according to the previous sequence.
But he who is surrounded by Maheśvara, when stepped upon by his foot,
beholds [the deity] who is red, blue, yellow, or white, whose left side is born of the three eyes,
and who is adorned with a crown of matted locks.
He has a crest of a garland of skulls and wears the crescent moon; he is embraced by the Viśvapadma-vajra, wears a crown, has a distorted face,
and is terrifying with his protruding fangs.
He is endowed with the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments, wears a tiger skin,
and bears a garland of human heads.
Adorned with a fresh necklace, a breast-ornament, earrings, and a crest-jewel,
along with the sacred thread and ashes— these are proclaimed as the six mudrās.
These six perfections are sealed with six seals.
In front of that is the Blessed Lady Padmaḍākinī, white in color, with one face, two arms, and three eyes; her hair is loose, she is naked, and she wears a girdle adorned with fragments.
With her left arm she embraces [him], holding a skull-cup filled with the blood of wicked Māras; threatening all directions with her lotus-hand that brandishes the gesture of menace,
she possesses a brilliance like the fire at the end of an aeon and delights in flowing blood.

Enveloping the two shanks, the Ḍākinīs and others previously mentioned— whose nature consists of great bliss and compassion and who bestow all accomplishments— should be placed in their respective positions upon the lotus and other seats.
The color and form are as previously described, but the Ḍākinī is white.
Khaṇḍarohā and Kṛṣṇā are the two goddesses; their colors are otherwise [than those of the central deity].
In her left hands she holds a khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup, and in her right hands a ḍamaru drum and a flaying knife.
Above the vase of the five nectars, in the intermediate directions, are vessels of the moon of bodhicitta.
At the eastern gate of the wheel of speech (vākcakra) is white Aṅgulikairāvatī of Kāmarūpa;
at the northern gate is red Vajrajaṭilamahābhairavā of Oḍra.
In the west, at Triśakuṇī, Mahāvīravāyuvegā is black;
in the south, at Kośalā, Vajrahūṃkārasurābhakṣī is green like the sky;
in the southeast, at Kaliṅga, Subhadraśyāmādevī is pale yellow.
In the southwest, at Lampāka, Vajrabhadra and Subhadrā are yellow.
[35] In the northwest, at Kāñcī, Mahābhairava and Hayakarṇā are green. (*22–23 missing) In the northeast, at Himālaya, Virūpākṣa and Khagānanā are sky-blue.
Bhūcarī belongs to the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*).
These heroes, Aṅkurika and the others, have one face, four arms, and three eyes; they wear matted hair and crowns, and are adorned with silken garments.
With two arms in an embrace, they hold a lotus and a bell; in the left hand is a *khaṭvāṅga*, and in the right is a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*).

The five mudrās [3], the goddesses beginning with Airāvatī, reside in the cardinal and intermediate directions; they stand in the ālīḍha posture, possess two arms and one face, hold an embrace and a skull-cup in their hands, and brandish the threatening gesture at the wicked.
A necklace, a crest-jewel, armlets, earrings, and the sacred thread;
the neck adorned with a garland of skulls, and a girdle with the sound of tinkling bells.
The previously mentioned female gatekeepers (dvārapālīs) should be present, as well as Kākāsyā and the others.
And in the foreign regions [5], there are the four deities beginning with Yamadāḍhī.
Upon the foreheads of all these heroes, with a garland of lotuses,
one should perform the meditation on the syllables as previously described, [placing] the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, along with the conceptualizations of mind, speech, and body.
The Lord of Mind is red in form; Speech is the syllable Oṃ, white; and Jaṃ Hūṃ is Kāyavajrā, the great light of the moon in the sky.
One should apply the nature of all the deities of the mandala to every state;
then, having beheld the wheel of gnosis, one should likewise join with it and worship it.
Having become the mother of all, one should meditate with one's entire being;
then, through the yoga of radiating and reabsorbing, one should [unify] mind, speech, and body in due order.
Oṃ śrī-vajra-ḍāka ārolik hūṃ phaṭ | ḍākinījālasaṃvara svāhā | [This is] the heart mantra.
Oṃ ārolik hrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ. This is the *upahṛdaya* (near-heart mantra).
Oṃ padmaḍākinī hrīḥ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. [This is] the heart mantra.
Oṃ sarvapadmaḍākinīye āḥ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This is the upahṛdaya (near-heart mantra).
Oṃ, to the ḍākinī, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ lāme hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ, to Rūpiṇī, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ phaṭ! Aṅkurika phaṭ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to Airāvatī, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ daha vajrajaṭila daha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ || [4] Oṃ mahābhairavīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ||
Oṃ, cook, O great hero! Cook, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ vāyuvege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, consume! Vajrahūṃkāra, consume! You who wear a garland of blood-stained entrails hanging down, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ surābhakṣī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ, seize, seize! Subhadra, seize the serpent-dragon dwelling in the seven netherworlds, or else threaten him, threaten him! Hūṃ, hūṃ, phaṭ!
Oṃ Śyāmādevī hūṃ 2 phaṭ.
Oṃ ākaṭya Vajrabhadra ākaṭya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ Subhadre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ hrīḥ Mahābhairava hrīḥ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ hayakarṇe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ || [7] Oṃ jñāṃ virūpākṣe jñāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ||
Oṃ khagānane hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ kākāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ ulukāsye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, to the dog-faced one, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, you whose face is like a boar’s snout, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ yamadāḍhī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ yamadūtī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ Yamamathanī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
One should perform the recitation according to the ritual procedure by means of the Pūjāsamayavajra;
thus, various rites—such as those for summoning and for nourishment—are accomplished.
He becomes a possessor of the Great Dharma, and the accomplishment of speech is attained.
Whether they be the highest, the middling, all, or the lowest and final—
those women of various excellent qualities remain with him,
impassioned by sensual desire, trembling, and overcome by the pain of longing.
They remain under the control of that very great-souled practitioner;
that auspicious great yogin shall wander within the abode of the universal lotus.
May the noble son of the Lord, whose nature is the supreme Dharma, dwell in Sukhāvatī.
At the time of rising, may he consume excrement, urine, and food;
may he become a king, a lord of knowledge, and a sovereign over the aggregate of Dharma.
Oṃ āḥ, homage to the heart; hiḥ,
svāhā to the head and the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa).
Vauṣaṭ hūṃ is the armor;
hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ is the eyes;
phaṭ haḥ is the weapon.
Vajradharma, Vairocana, Padmanṛtyeśvara, Vajrabhairava, Vajrasūrya, and Paraśu.
The specific colors—smoky, yellow, white, blue, red, crimson, and green—[are as follows]:
Oṃ Hrīṃ, Padmaḍākinī at the navel;
Hāṃ Āṃ Yāṃ, Padmayāminī.
Hrīṃ moṃ Padmamohanī;
Hre hrīṃ Padmasaṃcāriṇī;
Hūṃ hūṃ Padmasaṃtrāsanī. [38]
*Phaṭ hūṃ padmacaṇḍikā*. [The mantras for] the heart, the head, the crest, the eyes, the armor, and the weapon.
[Their colors are] red, blue, white, yellow, green, smoky, and grey.
At the end of the recitation, having placed [the deity], let him dwell at ease. The Heroine Yoginī, abiding in the state of all things,
remained silent and composed, taking recourse in the movement of speech.
Through the yoga with one's own tutelary deity, one should conceptualize all phenomena.
Urine is Vairocana, and marrow is combined with honey and clarified butter;
through the yoga of the tongue-samaya, there is indeed the gnosis of the heart.
Having meditated upon the Lord in his crown, the wise one should consume the food;
he becomes possessed of a divine form, born from Kāmadeva,
and by taking milk as a post-digestive drink, he is freed from old age and disease.
The goddess Gaṇikā is sung; she awakens beings through affection for sentient beings, having made the welfare of beings her supreme goal among all dharmas.
Relying upon the perfection of vigor and with a mind born of compassion, one should teach the secret dharmas; thus, the unsurpassed accomplishment of speech is attained.
To him, the teacher and liberator for the benefit of all sentient beings through the impelling of the reality of the Yoginīs,
they— eyes wide with wonder at the time of the various kinds of worship— offered praise.
Āḥ! O most excellent tree, the bliss of supreme passion, the pledge of non-dual bliss!
Delight, delight, hoḥ! O Lord of the bliss of supreme passion, perform the equal conduct!
Through the peaceful nature of the Sugata, counteract and transform by means of lotus-networks that bestow supreme passion!
Yawn, O you who long for the delights of love, with your clusters of lotus-like limbs!
Dance, O means of attaining that bliss, with your clusters of lotus-like limbs!
Rejoice, O Lord of Love, with the nets of the entire universe!
Hoḥ hāḥ hūṃ hāḥ [2] hoḥ hoḥ.
Victory to you, O Great Bliss! O producer of radiance! Delight, delight! Hoḥ!
O you whose bliss is the banner of passion, O you whose bliss is manifold and diverse splendor!

Victory, O bearer of splendor! Ha ha hā hoḥ! O supreme great bliss, hoḥ hūṃ hoḥ! O you who transcend sexual union, O bliss of passion, O supreme glory of the goddess Rati who triumphs through passion, hoḥ!
Hoḥ! Great bliss, the cause of supreme delight!
Hoḥ! Bliss! Hūṃ! Hoḥ! Delight in the manifold flames of the universe;
O great passion of the universe, bliss of the limbs and mind, supreme great bliss! Hoḥ!
Embrace bliss, Hoḥ! O supreme union of passion, Āḥ!
Ārolik Āḥ! Grasp great bliss, Hoḥ!
While this is being sung during the union of passion,
one quickly attains the perfection of great bliss consisting of mind, which is true happiness,
having presided over the great maṇḍala of the assembly.
The second chapter, the Abhidhānottara, [concerning] the *Mahāsuratapadmajālasamvara*.
